paragraphs: This paper asks how a language model can improve an answer by examining its own earlier response. It studies self-correction as a form of in-context learning: the model uses information within the ongoing interaction to refine its output. The theoretical analysis uses a simplified setting resembling an alignment task.

The central result is conditional. When the model’s self-examinations provide relatively accurate rewards, the authors show that it can refine responses through context. Their construction also explains roles for softmax attention, multiple attention heads, and the transformer’s multilayer perceptron block. This connects the analysis to architectural components used in realistic transformers, extending beyond theories restricted to simplified linear versions.

The authors validate their findings on synthetic datasets and introduce Checking as Context, a self-correction strategy inspired by the analysis. They apply it to reducing social bias and resisting jailbreaks. These results support a specific account of self-correction in which sufficiently informative self-evaluation helps guide improvement; the accuracy of that evaluation remains central to the theoretical claim.
neurips-2024-a-theoretical-understanding.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how relatively accurate self-evaluation can enable language models to improve responses through in-context learning.

paragraphs: Understanding actions in video involves both identifying what happens during observed footage and predicting what will happen afterward. These are usually studied as temporal action segmentation and long-term action anticipation, with separate models for each. ActFusion combines them in one diffusion model so that learning about observed actions and future actions can support each other.

The method organizes training around visible and hidden portions of a video sequence. The visible portion supplies the segmentation task. A later portion is deliberately masked, and learnable tokens replace its frames, giving the model a way to learn future prediction within the same training setup. This anticipative masking makes the distinction between the two tasks part of a shared sequence problem.

Experiments report benefits in both directions: joint learning improves segmentation as well as anticipation. On the 50 Salads, Breakfast, and GTEA benchmarks, ActFusion achieves state-of-the-art performance and surpasses task-specific models on both tasks. The findings show that this shared formulation can improve both capabilities while using a single model.
neurips-2024-actfusion-a-unified-diffusi.tldr: ActFusion jointly learns to label observed video actions and anticipate future ones, improving both tasks in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Video anomaly detection aims to identify unusual events in settings such as surveillance, traffic monitoring, industry, and healthcare. This paper combines a concise review of the field with a new dataset. The review examines models and datasets together, emphasizing that the data available for training and evaluation strongly influence what a detection model can learn.

A central issue identified by the review is the shortage of comprehensive datasets covering varied scenarios. The authors introduce Multi-Scenario Anomaly Detection, or MSAD, with 14 scenarios recorded from different camera views. Its footage includes diverse motion patterns and variations in lighting and weather, bringing several sources of visual change into the same dataset.

The paper also analyzes recent representative models using MSAD. This links the review’s concerns about dataset diversity to an evaluation resource that exposes models to more varied surveillance conditions. The authors highlight MSAD’s potential to help address anomaly detection across changing environments, positioning dataset development as an active part of advancing the field.
neurips-2024-advancing-video-anomaly-det.tldr: A review of video anomaly detection introduces MSAD, a dataset spanning 14 scenarios with varied viewpoints, motion, lighting, and weather.

paragraphs: The Schrödinger Bridge problem connects optimal transport with diffusion modeling. One approach to solving it, Iterative Markovian Fitting, repeatedly alternates between two projections of a continuous-time random process. Although this provides a useful modeling framework, generating an output can require hundreds of numerical steps for stochastic differential equations, making inference slow.

The authors introduce Discrete-time Iterative Markovian Fitting to change what the model learns. Instead of learning a continuous-time process that must later be simulated through many small steps, it learns a few transition probabilities at discrete times. The procedure can be implemented naturally with Denoising Diffusion GAN, connecting the proposed formulation to an established adversarial generative modeling technique.

For unpaired domain translation, the authors show that the discrete procedure can match the quality of the original approach while using only several generation steps. The contribution therefore joins a reformulation of the fitting procedure with a practical implementation route. Its stated result is a substantial reduction in generation steps without losing translation quality in the demonstrated comparison.
neurips-2024-adversarial-schrodinger-bri.tldr: Discrete-time bridge fitting can match continuous-time IMF’s unpaired translation quality using several generation steps instead of hundreds.

paragraphs: Flow-based generation connects noise and images through trajectories described by differential equations. Rectified flow and reflow speed up generation by progressively straightening these trajectories, treating the connection between each noise sample and image as approximately constant-velocity motion. This paper argues that such modeling has difficulty accurately learning the intended pairings when flows cross.

Constant Acceleration Flow replaces the constant-velocity description with a simple constant-acceleration equation. It also introduces two techniques intended to improve estimation: conditioning the acceleration model on initial velocity, and applying a reflow process to the initial velocity. Together, these changes address both the form of the trajectory and how its starting motion is estimated.

Comparative studies report improvements over rectified flow with reflow in speed and accuracy, alongside better preservation of the noise–image coupling. That last finding concerns whether the learned process maintains the intended pairing between its starting noise and resulting image. The results support constant acceleration as a useful alternative for fast generation with few steps.
neurips-2024-constant-acceleration-flow-.tldr: Constant Acceleration Flow improves reported generation speed, accuracy, and noise–image pairing preservation by changing how generative trajectories are modeled.

paragraphs: Some structured data depend on several interacting graphs, creating a need to process relationships across multiple domains together. Existing approaches largely use discrete graph filtering operations. This paper develops Continuous Product Graph Neural Networks, called CITRUS, from a framework based on tensorial partial differential equations on graphs.

CITRUS uses a mathematical property of continuous heat kernels on Cartesian graph products: they can be separated into components associated with the constituent graphs. The authors exploit this separability to implement graph spectral decomposition efficiently. This ties the network’s computation to a continuous mathematical description while making the combined graph structure more manageable.

The paper analyzes how CITRUS responds to changes in individual domain graphs and examines over-smoothing, where processing can make representations excessively similar. It also studies how graph spectra affect performance. Evaluations on traffic and weather forecasting datasets report better performance than existing approaches. The contribution combines a principled construction, theoretical analysis of its behavior, and evidence on spatiotemporal prediction tasks.
neurips-2024-continuous-product-graph-ne.tldr: CITRUS uses continuous equations on interacting graphs to support efficient modeling and improve reported traffic and weather forecasts.

paragraphs: Continual pre-training can deepen a language model’s knowledge of a domain such as mathematics or code. A practical challenge is choosing how much domain material to mix with general text. Testing many mixture ratios consumes substantial training resources, and the best ratio among those tested may still miss a better choice.

The paper proposes D-CPT Law, a scaling-law approach that fits relationships between training choices and performance using a limited set of small-scale experiments. The fitted law predicts both general and domain performance for different mixture ratios, model sizes, and dataset sizes. These predictions are intended to guide mixture selection without separately training every candidate configuration.

The authors also introduce a cross-domain extension that predicts the law for a target domain with about 1% of normal training costs spent on that domain. Experiments across six downstream domains support the effectiveness and generalizability of both versions. The findings position performance prediction as a practical tool for allocating continual pre-training effort and choosing data mixtures.
neurips-2024-d-cpt-law-domain-specific-c.tldr: D-CPT Law predicts continual pre-training performance to guide general-versus-domain data mixtures using limited small-scale experiments.

paragraphs: Intervention target estimation seeks to identify where an intervention acted within a causal system. Existing methods can struggle to share information across intervention instances or use labeled examples effectively. As a result, even modest changes to the data or causal graph may require estimating the targets again.

DeepITE approaches this problem with a variational graph autoencoder. Its framework learns jointly from examples involving different intervention targets and different causal graphs, using unlabeled data alone or combining it with labels. By learning across these examples, the model can identify targets in previously unseen samples and new causal graphs through inference, without retraining.

In the reported tests, DeepITE surpasses 13 baseline methods on Recall@k, a measure of target recovery among a selected set of candidates. It also provides fast inference, particularly for large graphs. Adding labels for 5–10% of the data substantially improves performance. These findings support the value of sharing learned information across intervention problems and incorporating even a modest amount of supervision.
neurips-2024-deepite-designing-variation.tldr: DeepITE learns across causal graphs and intervention examples to identify new intervention targets quickly, with further gains from limited labels.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a large three-dimensional CT image with diffusion models presents a difficult tradeoff. Training directly on whole volumes demands considerable memory, time, and data. Methods that instead learn from individual two-dimensional slices can lose consistency between slices, producing artifacts along the volume’s depth axis even when handcrafted cross-slice constraints are added.

DiffusionBlend learns a prior from three-dimensional patches and blends diffusion scores in a position-aware way. This gives the reconstruction method access to local three-dimensional structure without requiring diffusion training on each entire high-dimensional volume. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first use of a three-dimensional patch diffusion prior for medical image reconstruction.

Experiments cover sparse-view and limited-angle CT, including volumes measuring 256 by 256 by 500. The authors report significant improvements over previous methods and state-of-the-art reconstruction performance, with computational efficiency that is better than or comparable to previous leading approaches. The findings support patch-based three-dimensional modeling as a practical route to stronger large-volume CT reconstruction.
neurips-2024-diffusionblend-learning-3d-.tldr: DiffusionBlend combines position-aware diffusion scores from 3D patches to improve large-volume CT reconstruction with competitive computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Generating a three-dimensional hairstyle requires both its overall shape and the fine geometry of many individual strands. This paper builds a representation that moves from sparse, smoothed guide hairs to densely populated strands with detailed curls and variation. Its hierarchy separates broad hairstyle structure from the higher-frequency details that give hair its texture.

The method uses the Discrete Cosine Transform to separate these components while avoiding oscillation problems associated with the standard Fourier transform on open curves. It selects guide strands through k-medoids clustering of smoothed dense strands. This selection is designed to preserve hairstyle characteristics more accurately than sampling guides from fixed scalp-map grids.

A variational autoencoder generates the hairstyle using an architecture inspired by geometric deep learning and implicit neural representations. It supports guide strands away from a fixed grid and can complete dense hair at different quantities and densities. Empirical evaluations show convincing guide and dense hair generation, including nuanced high-frequency details, supporting the representation’s ability to carry structure across both levels.
neurips-2024-doubly-hierarchical-geometr.tldr: A hierarchical hairstyle representation combines carefully selected guide strands with fine geometric detail to generate dense 3D hair at flexible densities.

paragraphs: Multi-channel images can contain different kinds of measurements depending on their source. Two satellites, for example, may both provide RGB channels while differing in their remaining channels. Models therefore need to handle varying channel configurations. This paper argues that treating all channels equally can encourage redundant features and overlook the distinct information each channel offers.

DiChaViT aims to make channel-adaptive vision transformers learn more diverse representations. Its training strategy favors sampling more distinct sets of channels. Additional regularization and initialization techniques encourage each channel to contribute new information. In the motivating example, channels beyond RGB could focus on information that the RGB measurements do not capture.

Experiments on the satellite and cell microscopy datasets CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat report gains of 1.5–5.0% over the state of the art. Many proposed improvements are independent of a particular architecture, allowing their use in other designs. The findings suggest that supporting variable channel inputs benefits from explicitly encouraging complementary features during training.
neurips-2024-enhancing-feature-diversity.tldr: DiChaViT encourages complementary information across image channels, improving reported satellite and microscopy results over leading methods.

paragraphs: FIFO-Diffusion is an inference method for extending text-conditioned video generation using a pretrained diffusion model, without additional training. Its central idea is to keep a queue of consecutive frames at increasing noise levels. Each iteration removes a fully denoised frame from the front and adds a new random-noise frame at the back.

This diagonal denoising arrangement lets noisier frames use cleaner frames as references. However, mixing noise levels in this way also creates a mismatch between training and inference. The authors introduce latent partitioning to reduce that mismatch and lookahead denoising to make use of the available cleaner-frame references.

Because the active queue can remain fixed in size, the method uses constant memory with respect to target video length for a given baseline model. It also supports parallel inference across multiple GPUs. Experiments on existing text-to-video baselines demonstrate promising results. The claim of infinite generation describes the procedure’s conceptual ability to keep extending the sequence, supported by a memory requirement that does not grow with total length.
neurips-2024-fifo-diffusion-generating-i.tldr: FIFO-Diffusion extends pretrained text-to-video models through a rolling denoising queue, enabling conceptually unbounded video length with constant memory.

paragraphs: This paper attributes part of diffusion models’ slow training to how images are paired with noise. Under the usual random mapping, many different images become mixed throughout noise space, complicating the denoising function the model must learn. Immiscible Diffusion changes these pairings before diffusion takes place.

The proposed strategy first assigns noise samples to images, then performs diffusion. One implementation minimizes the total distance between paired images and noise samples within a mini-batch. This preferentially pairs images with nearby noise while preserving the Gaussian noise distribution. The physics analogy concerns making different sources less mixed, giving the model a more organized denoising problem.

To reduce assignment overhead, the authors use a quantized assignment strategy. Experiments report training speedups of up to threefold across the described diffusion-model settings, including unconditional and class-conditional training and fine-tuning. Their analysis also reports improved fidelity. The contribution is a small change to the training procedure whose reported benefit comes from organizing noise–data associations before learning.
neurips-2024-immiscible-diffusion-accele.tldr: Immiscible Diffusion assigns noise to images before diffusion, reporting up to threefold faster training alongside improved fidelity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a neural architecture for predicting Density Functional Theory Hamiltonians while incorporating their self-consistent nature. Traditional machine learning predictors often overlook that property. The proposed Deep Equilibrium Density Functional Theory Hamiltonian framework, or DEQH, makes self-consistency part of the model architecture through a deep equilibrium model.

The equilibrium component uses fixed-point solving to iteratively obtain the Hamiltonian. This gives DEQH a role as a solver as well as a predictor: its computation seeks an equilibrium rather than merely producing an output in a conventional prediction pass. The framework can combine this mechanism with existing Hamiltonian prediction models and avoids DFT calculations during training specifically to introduce self-consistency.

DEQHNet, an implementation of the framework, shows significantly improved prediction accuracy on MD17 and QH9. Ablation studies further examine the network’s effectiveness. The findings support embedding self-consistency directly into Hamiltonian learning, with the architectural approach addressing computational bottlenecks associated with introducing that property through DFT calculations for large or complex systems.
neurips-2024-infusing-self-consistency-i.tldr: DEQH embeds fixed-point solving into Hamiltonian prediction to capture self-consistency and improve reported accuracy without training-time DFT calculations for that purpose.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a probability distribution from samples under differential privacy, measuring error with Wasserstein distance. This distance reflects where probability mass is located: for a geographic population estimate, a small error means roughly placing people in the right areas. The goal is to adapt estimation quality to the difficulty of the particular distribution.

The authors formalize instance optimality through comparisons with algorithms given extra information. On the real line, the comparison algorithm knows that the distribution is one of two candidates whose densities differ by at most a factor of two. In two dimensions, the comparison algorithm receives a constant-factor approximation to the density.

For both settings, the paper characterizes instance-optimal estimation rates and gives algorithms that achieve them uniformly up to polylogarithmic factors. The two-dimensional approach proceeds through hierarchically separated trees, allowing extension to arbitrary metric spaces. A special case also yields instance-optimal learning of discrete distributions in total variation distance. These results provide privacy-preserving guarantees that respond to individual distribution difficulty.
neurips-2024-instance-optimal-private-de.tldr: The paper develops differentially private density estimators that adapt to individual distributions and achieve instance-optimal rates up to polylogarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Federated learning often relies on edge devices with limited computing resources and low-bandwidth connections to a central server. This paper proposes reducing numerical precision in both local training and model communication. High-precision computation is retained for the server’s aggregation step, concentrating that work where client models are combined.

The authors find that suitable server aggregation can recover high-precision models from low-precision local models. They provide a theoretical convergence result showing that their proposed paradigm can approach the optimal solution as training continues. The approach can also be incorporated into existing federated learning algorithms, offering a way to reduce client workload and communication costs.

Across the reported benchmarks, models trained with precision as low as eight bits perform comparably to models trained at full precision. The authors also find that low-precision local training can reduce local overfitting. With heterogeneous client data, such overfitting can push clients’ models farther apart and undermine aggregation, so this effect addresses an additional difficulty beyond resource consumption.
neurips-2024-low-precision-local-trainin.tldr: Low-precision client training and communication, paired with high-precision server aggregation, produce competitive federated models while reducing resource demands.

paragraphs: Visualization-of-Thought is a prompting method intended to improve spatial reasoning in language models. It draws inspiration from the human ability to imagine objects and actions that are not directly visible. The method asks models to visualize their reasoning traces so that these representations can guide later steps in the same problem.

The authors evaluate this approach on tasks requiring several connected spatial reasoning steps in two-dimensional grid worlds. These include navigation described through natural language, visual navigation, and visual tiling. The shared idea is that making intermediate spatial relationships explicit can provide useful context as reasoning proceeds through a sequence of decisions.

Experiments show significant improvements in the language models’ spatial reasoning, and the prompted models outperform existing multimodal language models on the evaluated tasks. The authors suggest that a similar approach may also be viable for multimodal models. The connection to a human mind’s eye serves as an inspiration and analogy for the prompting strategy, while the demonstrated findings concern performance on the grid-world tasks.
neurips-2024-mind-s-eye-of-llms-visualiz.tldr: Visualization-of-Thought prompting improves reported spatial reasoning by having language models visualize intermediate reasoning to guide subsequent steps.

paragraphs: Normalized cut is a difficult clustering problem whose objective contains ratios. That structure makes fractional programming a natural candidate for solving it. However, existing transformations have important restrictions: Dinkelbach’s transform handles a single ratio and is limited here to two-class clustering, while the quadratic transform handles several ratios but does not make this problem tractable.

The paper extends the quadratic transform to a multidimensional ratio setting. This reformulates the fractional problem with binary decisions as a bipartite matching problem, which can be solved through an iterative procedure. The key contribution is therefore a transformation that connects the original clustering objective to a form that supports manageable computation.

The authors also investigate the relationship between their method and minorization-maximization theory to verify convergence. This supplies theoretical support for the iterative process alongside the new reformulation. The stated advance addresses both obstacles highlighted in the abstract: handling the richer ratio structure of normalized cuts and obtaining a tractable form for the resulting optimization.
neurips-2024-multidimensional-fractional.tldr: A multidimensional fractional-programming transformation turns normalized-cut clustering into an iterative bipartite matching problem with convergence support.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models perform both visual recognition, such as locating objects, and higher-level understanding, such as answering image questions. The paper argues that handling both through token-by-token output generation misses opportunities. Recognition can be performed in parallel, and its results can supply useful information for subsequent understanding.

Octopus divides these roles across the language model’s layers. Lower layers perform parallel recognition using object queries, a mechanism associated with the Detection Transformer. The recognition results then pass to upper layers, which carry out sequential understanding. The authors find that object queries work well within language-model layers, making this division possible within the proposed framework.

Empirical studies report improved accuracy on popular multimodal language-model tasks and visual grounding speeds up to five times faster. The speed claim specifically concerns grounding, while the accuracy findings cover the evaluated tasks more broadly. The results support an architecture in which early parallel recognition both accelerates visual processing and informs the later sequential reasoning process.
neurips-2024-octopus-a-multi-modal-llm-w.tldr: Octopus performs visual recognition in parallel before sequential understanding, improving reported accuracy and accelerating grounding by up to fivefold.

paragraphs: Learning what people prefer depends on obtaining useful human feedback, and high-quality annotations can be costly. This paper studies how to choose the questions used to gather that feedback efficiently. Its focus is the information-gathering policy: which collections of items should be presented to people when learning a preference model.

The authors generalize optimal design methods to lists of items representing potential questions and answers. Their policy assigns a probability to each list, and feedback is collected from lists in proportion to those probabilities. This makes the choice of annotation questions an explicit optimization problem, connecting the data collection procedure to the preference model being learned.

The framework covers both absolute feedback about items and ranking feedback within a list. The authors develop efficient algorithms for both settings and analyze them, then evaluate their practicality on existing question-answering problems. The contribution is a common approach to selecting informative preference queries across these feedback formats, motivated by the expense of gathering high-quality human annotations.
neurips-2024-optimal-design-for-human-pr.tldr: The paper extends optimal experimental design to selecting informative lists of questions and answers for efficient human preference collection.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can help reinforcement-learning agents learn more from their existing experience. Much previous work has focused on agents that observe images, using changes such as cropping or shifting. This paper studies state-based continuous control, where agents directly receive kinematic and task features, and explores augmentation through Euclidean symmetries such as rotations.

The authors identify a representation problem: the joint-configuration features used by existing benchmarks are not well suited to these transformations. They advocate describing the configuration of limbs instead, treating limbs as rigid bodies connected by joints. This representation provides richer opportunities to construct augmented data through Euclidean transformations.

With minimal hyperparameter tuning, the proposed approach significantly improves both data efficiency and asymptotic performance across a wide range of continuous-control tasks. Data efficiency concerns how effectively the agent learns from available experience, while asymptotic performance concerns its eventual performance. The findings connect augmentation quality to the choice of state representation: suitable geometric features make these transformations useful for learning.
neurips-2024-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Representing control states through limb configurations enables geometric data augmentation that improves reported learning efficiency and eventual performance.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution benchmarks often treat any sample with a new label as unfamiliar. Yet a new label can describe content very close to the training distribution, making the boundary ambiguous. This paper examines that gradual transition by evaluating how far test examples depart from familiar data in meaning and in other visual properties.

The authors introduce Incremental Shift OOD, which groups test samples by degrees of semantic and covariate shift. Their Language Aligned Image feature Decomposition method supplies the shift measurements used for this division. They also construct Synthetic Incremental Shift, a generated-image dataset that adds more diverse covariate content to complement the benchmark.

Evaluation reveals that most tested detectors improve substantially as semantic differences increase. Some, including GradNorm, depend less on semantic shift, suggesting different detection mechanisms. Strong covariate changes can also cause some methods to classify images as unfamiliar. These findings show why aggregate detection scores benefit from examining the type and degree of change present in test data.
neurips-2024-rethinking-the-evaluation-o.tldr: New benchmarks separate degrees of semantic and covariate shift, revealing how different distribution changes influence out-of-distribution detectors.

paragraphs: Translating text on a film poster or album cover involves preserving visual design as well as linguistic content. Letterforms and styling help convey emotion, atmosphere, and theme. This paper introduces Multimodal Style Translation and the MuST-Bench benchmark to evaluate whether visual text generation models can transfer that design intent across different writing systems.

Initial experiments find that existing models struggle because written style descriptions do not adequately convey the visual design. The proposed SIGIL framework removes the need for those descriptions. It combines a multilingual glyph representation, pretrained variational autoencoders for stable style guidance, and optical character recognition with reinforcement-learning feedback to improve character readability.

SIGIL outperforms the evaluated baselines in style consistency and legibility while maintaining visual fidelity. The result addresses the task’s intertwined requirements: translated characters need to remain readable and retain the source design’s visual qualities. The publicly released benchmark provides a shared evaluation resource for investigating this broader form of translation, where appearance is part of what must be carried across languages.
neurips-2024-towards-visual-text-design-.tldr: MuST-Bench evaluates cross-language visual text design transfer, while SIGIL improves style preservation and readability without written style descriptions.

paragraphs: Direct speech-to-speech translation aims to turn spoken input into speech in another language. Such end-to-end systems often struggle to outperform cascades that connect speech recognition, text translation, and speech synthesis. The paper attributes this difficulty to the complexity of the direct task and a shortage of suitable training data.

TransVIP uses diverse datasets in a cascade-like training framework while enabling end-to-end inference through a joint-probability formulation. It also introduces two separate encoders to preserve the source speaker’s voice characteristics and isochrony, or speech timing. These design choices bring translation, voice identity, and temporal alignment into the same system.

Experiments on French–English translation show that TransVIP outperforms the current state-of-the-art speech-to-speech model in the reported comparison. Its emphasis on voice and timing makes it especially relevant to video dubbing, where translated speech must fit an existing audiovisual presentation. The contribution combines a way to use diverse training data with architectural support for retaining these source-speech properties during direct translation.
neurips-2024-transvip-speech-to-speech-t.tldr: TransVIP combines diverse-data training with direct speech translation and separate encoders for preserving voice characteristics and timing.

paragraphs: Snapshot compressive imaging recovers a three-dimensional data cube from one two-dimensional measurement, supporting applications such as video and hyperspectral imaging. This paper studies recovery with untrained neural networks, including deep image priors. Such methods are attractive because they may avoid costly retraining when the source model or measurement setup changes.

The authors develop a theoretical framework describing the performance of these recovery methods. It supports optimization of data-modulating masks and connects the number of frames recoverable from a single measurement to the untrained network’s parameters. This links the imaging setup and network choice to a fundamental question about how much information can be reconstructed.

The paper also adapts bagged deep image priors into SCI Bagged Deep Video Prior algorithms to address challenges in standard untrained-network solutions. In video experiments, the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance among untrained methods. With noisy measurements, it also outperforms supervised solutions in the reported tests. The work therefore contributes both recovery theory and an algorithm with demonstrated benefits under measurement noise.
neurips-2024-untrained-neural-nets-for-s.tldr: The paper analyzes untrained neural networks for snapshot reconstruction and introduces a bagged video-prior method with strong reported noisy-measurement results.
